answer:
**Mini-batch gradients should reflect the training population instead of a repetitive ordering artifact.** Suppose data is stored with all negative examples followed by all positives. Early batches push the model one way, later batches push it another, and momentum carries those order-dependent effects across updates. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

Shuffling mixes examples so batches are usually more representative and changes which examples interact in each update. It also prevents every epoch from repeating the same sequence of gradient errors. Sampling without replacement within an epoch is not exactly IID sampling, but it is a useful practical approximation for many objectives.

**Keep structure that the task needs.** Shuffle independent examples, not tokens inside a sentence or frames inside a sequence. Preserve grouping when labels or hidden state depend on order. In distributed training, update the sampler's epoch seed so workers do not repeat one permutation indefinitely.

Shuffling cannot fix an unrepresentative dataset or a leaked validation split. Use a reproducible seed when debugging, then distinguish order sensitivity from genuine model quality through appropriate validation.

**Technical details and references.**

Shuffling reduces systematic correlations between successive minibatches, such as batches containing only one class or time period. It makes minibatch gradients more representative and reduces order-specific training artifacts. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

Shuffling is without-replacement sampling within an epoch, not exactly iid sampling, but usually works well. It does not repair a biased dataset or invalid validation split. In distributed training, vary the sampler's epoch seed so every epoch does not repeat one order. Preserve group/sequence structure when the model or objective depends on it, and record seeds for reproducibility.
